theme: The Son above angels; the founder of salvation
readingInstruction: Read Hebrews 1:1-2:18 in one sitting if you can. Hebrews does not begin like a letter. It begins like a sermon, and it starts by announcing who Jesus is. As you read, count the ways the author describes the Son and notice how often he quotes the Old Testament to prove it. Don’t worry about catching every reference. Let the weight of the opening sentence settle on you.
settingTheScene: We are about to begin a book unlike any other in the New Testament. Hebrews has no greeting, no named author, and no named recipients. It opens with a single, majestic sentence in Greek and moves quickly into a sustained argument. The original readers were Jewish Christians who were under pressure. They were tempted to retreat from Christ and return to the safer, more familiar patterns of Moses and the temple. The author’s response is not to scold them first but to show them Jesus. Everything depends on seeing that the Son is better than anything they might be tempted to go back to. For us, the book is a gift because it explains, from the inside, how the entire Old Testament points to Christ.
observation: God spoke “long ago” by the prophets in many portions and ways, but “in these last days” by his Son (1:1-2).
The Son is heir of all things and the agent through whom the world was made (1:2).
He is “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature,” and he upholds the universe by his word (1:3).
After making purification for sins, he “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (1:3).
Hebrews 1:5-13 strings together seven Old Testament quotations to show that the Son is superior to angels.
Hebrews 1:8 applies the word “God” to the Son: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.”
Hebrews 2:1-4 is the first of several warnings: “we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard.”
Hebrews 2:14-18 explains that the Son shared in flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy the devil and free those who feared death.
interpretation:
The first four verses of Hebrews are one of the most compressed statements of Christology in the Bible. The author begins with a contrast that organizes the whole book: God spoke before, and God has now spoken in a final way. The prophets were real messengers with real messages, delivered in pieces and fragments. But the Son is not another fragment. He is the full and final word. Everything the prophets pointed toward has now arrived in a person.

Then come the seven descriptions of the Son. He is heir, which means everything belongs to him. He is the agent of creation, which echoes John 1 and Colossians 1. He is the radiance of God’s glory, like light that streams from the sun and shares its nature. He is the exact imprint of God’s being, like the impression stamped by a seal. He sustains all things by his powerful word. He made purification for sins. And he sat down. That last detail matters: a priest in the old covenant never sat, because the work was never finished. Christ sat because his work was done.

Having established who the Son is, the author turns to prove it from Scripture, and he starts with angels. This may seem odd to us, but in Jewish thought angels were awesome mediators of God’s law (see Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19). To say the Son is greater than angels is to say he is greater than the mediation that came through them. The seven quotations in chapter 1 are drawn from the Psalms and the prophets, and they are all applied to Jesus. The most striking is verse 8, where the Father himself says to the Son, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” The Father addresses the Son as God.

Chapter 2 opens with a warning that the author will repeat in different forms. If the message delivered through angels was binding and every transgression received a just penalty, how can we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? Notice the verb. The danger is not primarily active rebellion but drifting. The slow, quiet neglect of Christ is how many people leave him.

The rest of chapter 2 turns from the Son’s glory to his humiliation, and it is a beautiful turn. How can the one who is greater than angels be made “for a little while lower than the angels”? Because he came to taste death for everyone. The one who made the world entered it, took on flesh and blood, and died. Verses 14-15 tell us why: to destroy the one who has the power of death, the devil, and to deliver those who all their lives were enslaved by fear. Fear of death is a master, and Christ has broken its power.

Verse 17 introduces a theme that will dominate the book: he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest. The Son who is God became truly human so he could represent us before God. He is not simply above us. He is with us, and he is for us.
connection: The seven descriptions in 1:1-4 echo Proverbs 8 and Wisdom language, Genesis 1 (creation by word), and Psalm 110:1 (the session at God’s right hand). The quotations in chapter 1 draw from Psalm 2, 2 Samuel 7, Deuteronomy 32, Psalm 45, Psalm 102, and Psalm 110, which is a sweep of the Old Testament’s royal and creation theology. Chapter 2 draws on Psalm 8, where humanity is crowned with glory and honor, and Hebrews shows that Jesus is the true Man who fulfills that calling. Later in the book, 2:17 prepares us for Hebrews 4:14-5:10 and 7:1-28.
application:
First, take the opening verse as a personal challenge: God has spoken. Do you treat his word as final? Resolve to read Scripture this week as the voice of the Son, not as a collection of tips.

Second, notice the warning about drifting. Few believers wake up one day and decide to abandon Christ. They stop praying, then stop reading, then stop gathering. Ask yourself which small habits are keeping you attentive to him, and which neglected habits are pulling you off course.

Third, if you fear death, in any of its forms, remember what verse 15 says. Christ has freed those who were enslaved. You can begin to say honestly that you are afraid and ask him to deal with it. He understands, and he has already won.

Fourth, take comfort that the Son is not embarrassed by you. Hebrews 2:11 says he is not ashamed to call you brother.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for speaking to you by his Son.
Ask him to keep you from drifting.
Ask him to open your ears to hear him.
